The present case arises out of FIR No. 202/2005 of Police Station Darya Ganj, registered on the complaint of Brij Mohan alleging that he was cheated of an amount of Rs. 6,00,000 by accused Anand Kumar Jain and co-accused Nemi Chand Jain in a loan transaction supported by three State vs Anand Kr Jain on 26 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/135455139/
1 cheques which were later dishonoured and were found to contain forged endorsements of "good for payment".
Co-accused Nemi Chand Jain has since been declared a proclaimed offender.
The present judgment concerns only accused Anand Kumar Jain.
2. In brief, the prosecution case is that in the year 2003 the complainant Brij Mohan was approached for a loan of Rs. 6,00,000 in favour of Nemi Chand Jain.
It is alleged that accused Anand Kumar Jain, who was then working with Jain Co-operative Bank, Darya Ganj, introduced Nemi Chand Jain to the complainant and joined in assuring repayment.

It is further alleged that in pursuance of this understanding, three post-dated cheques of Rs. 2,00,000 each, drawn on account no. 2105 in the name of M/s Mahavir Impex, Punjab and Sind Bank, New Friends Colony, were issued in favour of M/s Jagdamba Road Lines Pvt. Ltd.
These cheques bore endorsements on the reverse side stating in substance that the cheques were good for payment with an apparent bank seal.
RAJ 3.
The complainant claims to have advanced Rs. 6,00,000 as a cash KUMAR SINGH loan against the said security.

Upon presentation of the cheques Digitally signed by RAJ KUMAR SINGH PS: Darya Ganj State Vs. Anand Kumar Jain through Syndicate Bank, Mori Gate Branch, the cheques were dishonoured with remarks of "funds insufficient" and with an intimation that the endorsements regarding bank guarantee were forged.

sentences.text: On these allegations, the complaint was lodged, and after investigation charge-sheet was filed for offences under Sections 420, 468 and 471 read with Section 34 IPC against the present accused.
As per the charge-sheet, no information could be gathered about co-accused Nemi Chand Jain and he was stated to be untraceable.
4. Cognizance of the offences was taken, copies of charge-sheet and relied upon documents were supplied to the accused in compliance with Section 207 CrPC.
After hearing the parties on the point of charge, the learned predecessor of this Court framed charge on 21.08.2010 against accused Anand Kumar Jain for offences under Sections 420/468/471/34 IPC.
The accused pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.
5. In order to prove its case, the prosecution examined ten witnesses.

6. PW1 Brij Mohan, the complainant, deposed that accused Anand Kumar Jain, then working with Jain Co-operative Bank, approached him in January 2003 for a loan of Rs. 6,00,000 for his cousin,
Nemi Chand Jain.
He stated that he met both accused and that accused Anand and Nemi Chand handed over three post-dated cheques of Rs. 2,00,000 each as security with bank guarantee.
PW1 further stated that he gave Rs. 6,00,000 in cash to accused RAJ KUMAR SINGH Digitally signed by RAJ KUMAR SINGH PS: Darya Ganj State Vs. Anand Kumar Jain Anand in the presence of Nemi Chand.
On presentation of the cheques in his own bank, he was informed that there were insufficient funds and that the bank endorsement of guarantee was fake.
He proved his written complaint Ex. PW1/A, the seizure memo of cheques Ex. PW1/B, the three cheques Ex. PW1/C1 to PW1/C3, and the bank return memos Ex. PW1/E1 to PW1/E4.

He stated that he had arranged Rs.
4,00,000 through "family friends"

PW1 also identified the arrest memo and personal search memo of accused Anand as Ex.
PW1/F and PW1/G.
There was no cross-examination of PW1 on behalf of the accused at that stage.

7. PW2 Rajender Prasad, an officer of Punjab and Sind Bank, New Friends Colony, produced the cheque returning register and proved entries relating to dishonour of two cheques for Rs. 2,00,000 each pertaining to account no. 2105, as Ex. PW2/A.
He confirmed that the cheques were returned unpaid.

8. PW3 HC Satish Chand, a police witness, joined the investigation on 18.08.2005 and deposed that he accompanied ASI Gyan Singh and the complainant to Jain Co-operative Bank where the complainant identified accused Anand, who was then arrested vide memo Ex. PW1/F and whose personal search was conducted vide memo Ex. PW1/G.

He also deposed to recording of the disclosure RAJ KUMAR SINGH Digitally signed by RAJ KUMAR SINGH PS: Darya Ganj State Vs.
Anand Kumar Jain statement Ex. PW3/A and taking specimen handwriting of accused Anand on 25 sheets Ex. PW3/B.
9.

PW4 Harbans Singh, the then Senior Manager of Punjab and Sind Bank, New Friends Colony,
stated that he handed over to police the bank statement of account no. 2105 in the name of M/s Mahavir Impex and a copy of a ration card, seized vide Ex. PW4/A.
In cross-examination he stated that he saw the accused for the first time in Court and that he did not know whether the accused had any direct or indirect role in opening the said account.

He specifically stated that there was no practice in their bank of writing endorsements such as "this cheque good for payment" on cheques and that the stamp and endorsement produced by police were not of their bank.

10. PW5 Kuldeep Singh, clerk of Punjab and Sind Bank, New Friends Colony, produced the cheque returning register for 2003 and proved entries relating to dishonour of cheque no. 4453 and cheque no. 4458 from account no. 2105 due to insufficient funds as Ex. PW5/A.
On being recalled later as PW5, he stated that record regarding cheque no. 4457 dated 09.06.2003 was not available.

In cross-examination he clarified that Ex. PW5/A only contained details of cheques dishonoured on 4,
5 and 6 June 2003 and that he could not say whether cheque no. 4457 was ever presented for encashment.

He further explained that where drawer and drawee are in the same bank, seal over leaf is normally not required, and RAJ KUMAR SINGH Digitally signed by RAJ KUMAR SINGH PS:

11. PW6 Narain Singh, retired SI and then Duty Officer, proved the registration of FIR on the basis of rukka presented by ASI Gyan Singh and proved FIR and endorsement as Ex. PW6/A and Ex.
PW6/B.

proved his opinion Ex. PW7/A and reasons Ex. PW7/B.

He deposed that on the basis of the material sent to him, the person who wrote the signatures marked A1 to A4 also wrote the signatures marked State vs Anand Kr Jain on 26 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/135455139/

He further clarified that it had not been possible to express any opinion on the remaining items on the material available.
The admitted signatures A1 to A4 were of "Nemi Chand Jain".
No opinion was given connecting any questioned writing to accused Anand Kumar Jain.

13. PW8 Inspector Sudhir Kumar, who took over investigation in September 2006, proved that he seized cheque bounce receipts vide Ex. PW1/D, examined the complainant, issued a notice to Punjab and Sind Bank Ex. PW8/A and received reply Ex. PW8/B which confirmed that the bank did not follow the practice of endorsing cheques as "good for payment".
He deposed that despite efforts he could not trace co-accused Nemi Chand, after which he completed the investigation and filed the charge-sheet.

In cross- RAJ KUMAR SINGH Digitally signed by RAJ KUMAR SINGH PS: Darya Ganj State Vs. Anand Kumar Jain examination he candidly admitted that the cheques were issued by Nemi Chand, that the cheques had already been sent to FSL by the previous IO and that at the time of arrest of the present accused there was no documentary proof of the alleged offence against him except the statement of the complainant.

sentences.text: 14. PW9 retired SI Gyan Singh, the initial Investigating Officer, proved the endorsement on the complaint Ex. PW9/A, his request letter to the bank Ex. PW9/B and the reply Ex. PW9/C.
He also proved seizure of the bank statement and account opening papers as Ex. PW9/D and Ex. PW9/E and seizure of specimen signatures of Nemi Chand as Ex. PW9/F and Ex. PW9/G.

He stated that he arrested accused Anand on 18.08.2005 near Jain Co-operative Bank at the instance of the complainant, recorded his disclosure statement and obtained his specimen handwriting on twenty five sheets Ex. PW3/B.

In cross-examination, PW9 admitted that the cheques in question were issued by Nemi Chand, that no bank official had stated anything against accused Anand and that at the time of arrest of the accused there was no documentary proof against him other than the complainant's statement.
He also admitted that he had not taken adverse orders from the Court against absconding co-accused Nemi Chand as his address could not be verified.

15. PW10 Sahil, an officer of Punjab and Sind Bank, New Friends Colony, appeared with reference to cheque no. 4453, cheque no.

16. The FSL forwarding and opinion from the Government Examiner of Questioned Documents,
Hyderabad, including the covering letter and opinion, form part of the record.
17. The statement of accused under Section 313 CrPC read with Section 281 CrPC was recorded on 19.11.2024.
The incriminating circumstances emerging from the evidence were put to him.

The accused denied all allegations and specifically stated that he had not introduced Nemi Chand to the complainant, had not received any money from the complainant, had not witnessed any handing over of cheques, and had not given any guarantee.

He asserted that the cheques did not bear his State vs Anand Kr Jain on 26 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/135455139/
4 handwriting or signature and that he had been falsely implicated in a dispute essentially between the complainant and Nemi Chand.
18. The accused chose to lead defence evidence and examined himself as DW1.

In his sworn testimony he reiterated that he had no role in the financial dealings between the complainant and Nemi Chand, that he had not stood surety or guarantor and had not signed any document in that regard.
He denied having introduced Nemi Chand to the complainant and denied handing over any cheques to the complainant.
In cross-examination he denied the prosecution suggestions and maintained his stand.
RAJ KUMAR SINGH Digitally signed by RAJ KUMAR SINGH PS:
Darya Ganj State Vs. Anand Kumar Jain 19.

entities.text: Darya Ganj State Vs. Anand Kumar Jain
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Defence counsel also filed written submissions on behalf of the accused, inter alia contending that the dispute was essentially civil in nature, that the main transaction was between the complainant and co-accused Nemi Chand, that there was no documentary material to show receipt of money by the present accused, that the FSL report did not connect any writing to the accused and that the investigation itself acknowledges absence of material against him.

20. An application moved earlier by the accused for recalling certain witnesses, including the complainant, under Section 311 CrPC/348 Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), was dismissed by this Court, and the said order stands affirmed by the Hon'ble High Court.
That aspect is relevant only to the procedural history.
It does not dispense with the duty of the prosecution to establish its case beyond reasonable doubt on the evidence already available.

21. In light of the charge and the rival submissions, the primary questions that arise are whether the prosecution has proved beyond reasonable doubt that the present accused, in furtherance of common intention with co-accused Nemi Chand, dishonestly induced the complainant to part with Rs. 6,00,000 and thereby committed cheating punishable under Section 420 read with Section 34 IPC.

Further, whether it is proved that the present accused, in furtherance of such common intention, made the alleged false endorsements "good for payment" and thereby forged the cheques in question with intent to cheat, so as to attract Section RAJ KUMAR SINGH Digitally signed by RAJ KUMAR SINGH PS: Darya Ganj State Vs. Anand Kumar Jain 468 IPC.

entities.text: Darya Ganj State Vs. Anand Kumar Jain 468
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Furthermore, whether it is proved that the present accused used the said cheques as genuine, knowing or having reason to believe them to be forged, so as to attract Section 471 IPC.
Finally, whether any constructive liability under Section 34 IPC can be fastened upon the accused in the absence of direct acts attributed to him.

22. The prosecution must first establish that the complainant parted with Rs. 6,00,000 and that such delivery of money was directly referable to inducement by the present accused, acting with dishonest intention at the inception of the transaction.
This is an essential ingredient of the offence of cheating.

State vs Anand Kr Jain on 26 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/135455139/
5 23.
On this aspect, the only substantive evidence is the oral testimony of PW1.

In his written complaint Ex. PW1/A, PW1 stated that he agreed to give Rs. 6,00,000 as loan to Nemi Chand at the request of accused Anand, that three cheques with proposed bank endorsement would be provided as security, and that he "gave a sum of Rs. 6 lacs to Mr. Nemi Chand Jain".

In his examination-in- chief before the Court, however, PW1 improved upon this version and stated that he gave Rs.
6,00,000 in cash to accused Anand in the presence of Nemi Chand.
This is a material inconsistency.

It goes to the root of the alleged role of the present accused and cannot be brushed aside merely because PW1 was not cross- examined at that time.
RAJ KUMAR SINGH
Digitally signed by RAJ KUMAR SINGH PS: Darya Ganj State Vs. Anand Kumar Jain 24.

entities.text: Darya Ganj State Vs. Anand Kumar Jain
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: PW1 has also stated that he arranged Rs. 4,00,000 from "family friends" and Rs. 2,00,000 from his own funds.

No friend has been examined, no record has been produced to show withdrawal of such amounts from any bank account, and no contemporaneous writing such as a receipt,
promissory note or even a simple acknowledgment has been brought on record, despite the admittedly substantial amount involved.
The complainant is a man of business.
In the ordinary course, a prudent person advancing such a sum on interest would either pay it through identifiable banking channels or would at least maintain some record.

The complete absence of any independent or documentary corroboration of the payment, when such corroboration could and should have been available, substantially weakens the prosecution version.
25.
It is also relevant that the investigation has not brought on record any material to show that any part of the alleged loan amount ever reached the present accused.
There is no bank statement showing any credit into his account, nor is there any evidence of direct benefit accruing to him.

PW9, the first Investigating Officer, in fact admits that at the time of arrest of the accused there was no documentary material against him except the statement of PW1.
26.

It is settled law that while a conviction can rest on the sole testimony of a truthful witness, such testimony must inspire confidence and must be consistent with the surrounding RAJ KUMAR SINGH Digitally signed by RAJ KUMAR SINGH PS: Darya Ganj State Vs. Anand Kumar Jain circumstances.

entities.text: Darya Ganj State Vs. Anand Kumar Jain
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The internal shift between the complaint and deposition regarding who received the money, the vague assertion about arranging funds without any corroboration, and the absence of any material showing that the accused benefited from the transaction, cumulatively create reasonable doubt about the precise role of the present accused in the alleged loan.
27. The fact that PW1 could not be cross-examined does not automatically elevate his testimony to unimpeachable truth.
The Court is still duty bound to examine whether that testimony is consistent with the earlier complaint, with the probabilities of the case, and with other evidence on record.

On this test, PW1's version regarding handing over of Rs. 6,00,000 to the present accused does not inspire such confidence as would justify returning a finding of guilty, especially after two decades of litigation.

State vs Anand Kr Jain on 26 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/135455139/
6 28.
The next set of allegations relate to the alleged forgery of cheques by making false endorsements "good for payment" with a forged bank stamp and the alleged use of such forged cheques as genuine.
29. The prosecution case itself proceeds on the basis that the cheques belonged to account no. 2105 of M/s Mahavir Impex and were signed by co-accused Nemi Chand.

This has been confirmed by PW4, PW5, PW8 and PW9, as well as by the FSL opinion which connects the admitted signatures of Nemi Chand with the RAJ KUMAR SINGH Digitally signed by RAJ KUMAR SINGH PS: Darya Ganj State Vs. Anand Kumar Jain signatures on the cheques.

entities.text: Darya Ganj State Vs. Anand Kumar Jain
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: There is no dispute that the signatures of the drawer on the cheques are those of Nemi Chand.

30. As regards the endorsements "good for payment", the bank witnesses have categorically deposed that Punjab and Sind Bank does not follow the practice of putting such endorsements on cheques and that the stamp appearing on the cheques is not of their bank.
Thus the endorsements are indeed suspect.

However, the core question in so far as the present accused is concerned is whether there is any reliable evidence that he either wrote those endorsements, or procured them to be written, or used the cheques containing such endorsements as genuine, with knowledge of their falsity.
31. It is here that the prosecution case against accused Anand becomes particularly fragile.

The Investigating Officer obtained specimen handwriting of the present accused on twenty five sheets Ex. PW3/B and got them examined along with the cheques by the Government Examiner of Questioned Documents.
The expert, as PW7, has given a clear and limited opinion.

He has linked the admitted signatures A1 to A4 of Nemi Chand with the signatures on the cheques marked Q1/1,
Q3/1 and Q5/1.
He has specifically stated that it has not been possible to express any opinion on the remaining items on the material available.
There is no expert opinion stating that any questioned writing or endorsement on the cheques is that of accused Anand.
RAJ KUMAR SINGH Digitally signed by RAJ KUMAR SINGH PS: Darya Ganj State Vs. Anand Kumar Jain 32.

entities.text: Darya Ganj State Vs. Anand Kumar Jain
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The prosecution has, therefore, failed to produce any scientific evidence connecting the present accused with the allegedly forged endorsements.
Nor has any bank official stated that the accused had authority to issue such endorsements, or that he in any manner dealt with these cheques in his official capacity.
On the contrary, PW4 has stated that he saw the accused for the first time in Court and that the stamp and endorsement are not of their bank.

33. The requirement of a "false document" as defined in Section 464 IPC, which underlies an offence under Section 468 IPC, mandates proof that the accused made or participated in the making of a document in such a manner that it falsely purports to have been made by or with the authority of someone who did not so make or authorise it.

Where the maker of the document is someone else and the prosecution does not establish that the present accused authored or authorised the impugned writing, the foundation for a charge of forgery against him is lacking.
The Supreme Court has emphasised that the person who is arraigned for forgery must be shown to be the "maker" of the false document in the sense explained in Section 464.

Reliance is placed on the judgments of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Mohammad Ibrahim Vs. State of Bihar (2009) 8 SCC 751 and Sheila State vs Anand Kr Jain on 26 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/135455139/

34.

In the present case, at the highest, it can be said that some endorsements purporting to be bank endorsements were written on RAJ KUMAR SINGH Digitally signed by RAJ KUMAR SINGH PS:
Darya Ganj State Vs. Anand Kumar Jain the cheques and that those endorsements were not genuine.

entities.text: Darya Ganj State Vs. Anand Kumar Jain
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The person whose handwriting appears thereon has not been identified.
The FSL opinion does not attribute those writings to the present accused.
There is also no evidence that the accused presented these cheques for encashment, or that he used them in any other fashion so as to attract Section 471 IPC.
The complainant's evidence is that the cheques were handed over as security and that he himself presented them through his bank.
This conduct, even if assumed, does not by itself prove that accused Anand made or used forged documents.
35. It is true that forgery can sometimes be established by circumstantial evidence.
However, such circumstances must point with reasonable certainty to the involvement of the accused in the making or use of the forged document.
A mere allegation that the accused accompanied the drawer or introduced him to the complainant, without more, cannot substitute for proof of authorship or use of the forged endorsement.
36. The charge against the present accused is also framed with the aid of Section 34 IPC.
Common intention cannot be presumed from relationship or association alone.
There must be some act or conduct from which a meeting of minds in respect of the specific criminal act can be inferred.

In the present case, apart from the complainant's assertion that accused Anand introduced Nemi Chand and handed over cheques, there is no independent material RAJ KUMAR SINGH Digitally signed by RAJ KUMAR SINGH PS: Darya Ganj State Vs. Anand Kumar Jain to show that the accused shared any common intention with Nemi Chand to cheat the complainant by forged endorsements.

entities.text: Darya Ganj State Vs. Anand Kumar Jain
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 37. The fact that co-accused Nemi Chand has remained untraced further restricts the evidentiary foundation available to the Court.

No material has been collected to show that accused Anand participated in planning the alleged endorsement, that he derived any share in the monies allegedly obtained, or that he took any steps to facilitate encashment of forged cheques.

The investigation, by the admission of PW9, proceeded to arrest him on the basis of the complainant's version alone,
without corroboration from bank officials.
In such circumstances, Section 34 IPC cannot be used as a mere device to extend liability in the absence of primary proof of wrongful acts attributable to the accused.
38. It has been argued on behalf of the prosecution that since the complainant's testimony remained unchallenged due to non-cross- examination, it should be read in full against the accused.
It is correct that non-cross-examination deprives the accused of an opportunity to test the witness.
However, it does not absolve the prosecution from its fundamental burden to establish all ingredients of the offences beyond reasonable doubt.
The Court is not compelled to accept a version which is internally inconsistent, uncorroborated on vital aspects and not supported by the surrounding circumstances.

8

sentences.text: The fact that an application under Section 311 CrPC was dismissed and that the dismissal was affirmed by the Hon'ble High Court only means that the evidence already recorded has to be appreciated as it stands.
It does not follow that any infirmity in that evidence is cured or that the prosecution is relieved of its obligation to prove its case on that material.
40. On an overall appraisal, the following features stand out.
There is no independent witness to the alleged loan transaction.
The source of Rs. 6,00,000 claimed to have been arranged by the complainant remains unproved, beyond his bare assertion about friends and personal funds.
No bank withdrawal, no friend, and no written acknowledgment of loan have been produced.
There is a material discrepancy between the written complaint, which states that money was handed to Nemi Chand, and the deposition, which states that money was handed to accused Anand.

The investigating officers themselves admit that no documentary material existed against the present accused at the time of his arrest beyond the complainant's word, and no bank official has deposed to any involvement of the accused in the relevant account or endorsements.
The FSL opinion connects the handwriting of co- accused Nemi Chand with the signatures on the cheques.
It expressly states that no opinion was possible on the remaining questioned writings.
There is, therefore, no expert basis to hold that the alleged forged endorsements "good for payment" were RAJ KUMAR SINGH Digitally signed by RAJ KUMAR SINGH PS: Darya Ganj State Vs.
Anand Kumar Jain made by the present accused
. There is also no evidence that he ever used those cheques as genuine, whether by presenting them or otherwise.
In these circumstances, the essential ingredients of offences under Sections 468 and 471 IPC, in so far as they relate to the present accused, are not made out.

41. For an offence under Section 420 IPC, the prosecution must establish deception, dishonest intention at the inception of the transaction, inducement, and delivery of property pursuant to such inducement.

In the present case, the uncorroborated and inconsistent testimony of PW1, tested against the admissions of the Investigating Officer and the absence of any direct benefit to the accused, does not establish beyond reasonable doubt that accused Anand Kumar Jain acted with dishonest intention at the inception of the transaction, or that he induced the complainant to part with money in the manner alleged.

42. It is a basic tenet of criminal jurisprudence that suspicion, however grave, cannot replace proof,
and that whenever two views are reasonably possible on the evidence, the view favourable to the accused must be adopted.

On the totality of the material discussed above, this Court is unable to hold that the prosecution has discharged its burden of proving the guilt of accused Anand Kumar Jain beyond reasonable doubt for any of the offences charged.

The benefit of doubt must, therefore,
enure to him.

opennyai_summary.issue:
21. In light of the charge and the rival submissions, the primary questions that arise are whether the prosecution has proved beyond reasonable doubt that the present accused, in furtherance of common intention with co-accused Nemi Chand, dishonestly induced the complainant to part with Rs. 6,00,000 and thereby committed cheating punishable under Section 420 read with Section 34 IPC.
Further, whether it is proved that the present accused, in furtherance of such common intention, made the alleged false endorsements "good for payment" and thereby forged the cheques in question with intent to cheat, so as to attract Section RAJ KUMAR SINGH Digitally signed by RAJ KUMAR SINGH PS: Darya Ganj State Vs. Anand Kumar Jain 468 IPC.
Furthermore, whether it is proved that the present accused used the said cheques as genuine, knowing or having reason to believe them to be forged, so as to attract Section 471 IPC.
Finally, whether any constructive liability under Section 34 IPC can be fastened upon the accused in the absence of direct acts attributed to him.
22. The prosecution must first establish that the complainant parted with Rs. 6,00,000 and that such delivery of money was directly referable to inducement by the present accused, acting with dishonest intention at the inception of the transaction.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
This is an essential ingredient of the offence of cheating.
The complete absence of any independent or documentary corroboration of the payment, when such corroboration could and should have been available, substantially weakens the prosecution version.
25.
It is settled law that while a conviction can rest on the sole testimony of a truthful witness, such testimony must inspire confidence and must be consistent with the surrounding RAJ KUMAR SINGH Digitally signed by RAJ KUMAR SINGH PS: Darya Ganj State Vs. Anand Kumar Jain circumstances.
The internal shift between the complaint and deposition regarding who received the money, the vague assertion about arranging funds without any corroboration, and the absence of any material showing that the accused benefited from the transaction, cumulatively create reasonable doubt about the precise role of the present accused in the alleged loan.
27. The fact that PW1 could not be cross-examined does not automatically elevate his testimony to unimpeachable truth.
33. The requirement of a "false document" as defined in Section 464 IPC, which underlies an offence under Section 468 IPC, mandates proof that the accused made or participated in the making of a document in such a manner that it falsely purports to have been made by or with the authority of someone who did not so make or authorise it.
Where the maker of the document is someone else and the prosecution does not establish that the present accused authored or authorised the impugned writing, the foundation for a charge of forgery against him is lacking.
7 Sebastian Vs. R Jawaharaj (2018) 7 SCC 581.
34.
This conduct, even if assumed, does not by itself prove that accused Anand made or used forged documents.
However, such circumstances must point with reasonable certainty to the involvement of the accused in the making or use of the forged document.
A mere allegation that the accused accompanied the drawer or introduced him to the complainant, without more, cannot substitute for proof of authorship or use of the forged endorsement.
Common intention cannot be presumed from relationship or association alone.
There must be some act or conduct from which a meeting of minds in respect of the specific criminal act can be inferred.
In the present case, apart from the complainant's assertion that accused Anand introduced Nemi Chand and handed over cheques, there is no independent material RAJ KUMAR SINGH Digitally signed by RAJ KUMAR SINGH PS: Darya Ganj State Vs. Anand Kumar Jain to show that the accused shared any common intention with Nemi Chand to cheat the complainant by forged endorsements.
No material has been collected to show that accused Anand participated in planning the alleged endorsement, that he derived any share in the monies allegedly obtained, or that he took any steps to facilitate encashment of forged cheques.
In such circumstances, Section 34 IPC cannot be used as a mere device to extend liability in the absence of primary proof of wrongful acts attributable to the accused.
However, it does not absolve the prosecution from its fundamental burden to establish all ingredients of the offences beyond reasonable doubt.
The Court is not compelled to accept a version which is internally inconsistent, uncorroborated on vital aspects and not supported by the surrounding circumstances.
RAJ KUMAR SINGH Digitally signed by RAJ KUMAR SINGH PS: Darya Ganj State Vs. Anand Kumar Jain 39.
The fact that an application under Section 311 CrPC was dismissed and that the dismissal was affirmed by the Hon'ble High Court only means that the evidence already recorded has to be appreciated as it stands.
It does not follow that any infirmity in that evidence is cured or that the prosecution is relieved of its obligation to prove its case on that material.
41. For an offence under Section 420 IPC, the prosecution must establish deception, dishonest intention at the inception of the transaction, inducement, and delivery of property pursuant to such inducement.
In the present case, the uncorroborated and inconsistent testimony of PW1, tested against the admissions of the Investigating Officer and the absence of any direct benefit to the accused, does not establish beyond reasonable doubt that accused Anand Kumar Jain acted with dishonest intention at the inception of the transaction, or that he induced the complainant to part with money in the manner alleged.
On the totality of the material discussed above, this Court is unable to hold that the prosecution has discharged its burden of proving the guilt of accused Anand Kumar Jain beyond reasonable doubt for any of the offences charged.
opennyai_summary.decision:
The benefit of doubt must, therefore,
enure to him.
Accused Anand Kumar Jain is acquitted of the offences punishable under Sections 420, 468 and 471 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code in FIR No. 202/2005, Police Station Darya Ganj.
